d.x: Three commands get you a dashboard with realistic data in it. The rest of this page is the four things you will actually do afterwards: import a report you already have, publish from a pipeline, send somebody a file, and decide where the data lives.

Test Hub is one Python package. It needs Python 3.11 or newer and nothing else — no Node, no database server, no container runtime. The dashboard is hand-written CSS and JavaScript shipped inside the wheel, so there is no build step to run and nothing to fetch from a CDN. shell From PyPI $ pip install test-hub That gives you the test-hub command, the test_hub import package and the Python publishing SDK. Storage is SQLite in a file, artifacts are a directory of files, and both are created on first use.

d.h: See it with data in it
d.x: An empty dashboard tells you nothing about whether you want one. test-hub demo invents a plausible organization — five projects across three teams, two weeks of history, real failures, genuinely flaky tests, and one run that is still going so the live indicator has something to show. Seed the sample data shell $ test-hub demo It prints what it made: output Real output, with the log lines trimmed seeding sample data… sample data created 5 projects, 31 runs, 258 test results, 270 attempts 23 failures and 12 flaky retries, so the red and amber states have something to show one run is still open: f0c9dd0b-4534-4e9c-8ede-844121dd118b stored in /private/tmp/th-docs-site next: test-hub serve Start the server shell $ test-hub serve output Test Hub http://127.0.0.1:8000 dashboard http://127.0.0.1:8

d.h: Publish from CI to a shared server
d.x: The same import, aimed at a server somebody else is running. publish is ingest over HTTP: same adapters, same parsing, same result object. shell $ export TEST_HUB_TOKEN='ths_…' # from `test-hub token create` $ test-hub publish results.xml \ --url https://test-hub.internal \ --project payments-api \ --team payments \ --type component \ --branch "$GIT_BRANCH" \ --commit "$GIT_COMMIT" \ --token-env TEST_HUB_TOKEN There is deliberately no --token flag. A token on a command line is visible in ps to every other user on the machine, lands in shell history, and appears in the CI log whenever a step is echoed. --token-env and --token-file are the two supported ways in. You do not need Test Hub installed on the build agent at all. This is a complete publisher: shell curl is a first-class client, not

By default, in the platform's user-data directory — not in whatever folder you happened to be standing in, so that test-hub serve run from two different projects is one Test Hub rather than two. Platform Default data directory macOS ~/Library/Application Support/test-hub Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/test-hub, or ~/.local/share/test-hub Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\test-hub Inside it: test-hub.db (SQLite, in WAL mode) and artifacts/ (content-addressed files). The directory is created with mode 0700 where the filesystem supports it. Override it with --data-dir or TEST_HUB_DATA_DIR, both of which mean the same thing. shell Keep an experiment out of your real store $ export TEST_HUB_DATA_DIR=/tmp/th-scratch $ test-hub demo --reset $ test-hub serve

A feature list is only useful if it says what the feature costs. This one gives the reason for each decision and names the tradeoff, so you can tell in advance whether Test Hub is the shape of tool you want.

d.h: One canonical model, whatever produced the results
d.x: Test Hub does not care what language your tests are written in, what framework ran them, or what started the run. Everything that arrives is normalized into one hierarchy: text test_hub.domain.models Workspace └── Project └── TestRun one execution of a suite of tests ├── TestSuite a file / class / feature grouping │ └── TestCase a test's identity within the run │ └── TestAttempt one execution of it (retries!) ├── Artifact a file produced by the run └── Event the append-only log the run was folded from These are Pydantic models carrying a schema_version, and they are the public wire contract. The SQLAlchemy rows on disk are a separate, private thing; nothing serializes an ORM object. That separation is what lets the table layout change — a new index, a split table, PostgreSQL — without a ve

d.h: Ten statuses, and the framework's own word beside every one
d.x: Every framework spells its outcomes differently. Test Hub stores exactly one normalized status per attempt and always keeps the original string next to it in TestAttempt.original_status. passed failed error skipped xfailed xpassed running queued cancelled unknown The normalization is a lookup table, not a heuristic. A word it does not recognise becomes unknown and raises a parser warning on the import; it never becomes passed by accident. The table and its exact behaviour are on the canonical schema page.

This is the decision the rest of the product is built on. A rerun produces a new TestAttempt with attempt_number incremented; the earlier attempt is preserved exactly as it was recorded. Nothing in Test Hub ever mutates an attempt. Two things follow. First, flakiness is observable — a test that failed and then passed is visibly a test that failed and then passed, not a green tick. Second, a retried test does not count twice: each test contributes once, through its last attempt, and its retry history stays available beside that. Why "last", not "best" or "worst" A test that failed and then passed on retry is green and flaky. A test that passed and then failed on a rerun is red. Both facts stay on the page; the count follows the last thing that actually happened.

A test's identity has to survive being re-run, re-ordered, re-parameterized in a different order, moved to a different line and executed on another machine. If it does not, every run invents a new set of tests, and history, comparison and flakiness are all worthless. Test Hub therefore derives a UUIDv5 from what the test is and never from when or where it ran: Part of the identity Deliberately excluded project key timestamps suite path line numbers, file offsets class name durations test name worker / shard id, hostname normalized parameters run id, build number, branch Named parameters are sorted by name, so (b=2, a=1) and (a=1, b=2) are one test. Rendered object addresses and bare UUIDs inside parametrized ids are scrubbed to stable tokens, because otherwise a framework that prints <Foo

Results appear in the browser within a couple of seconds without a refresh. The transport is Server-Sent Events rather than WebSockets because the traffic is entirely one-way, and SSE gives three things for free that would otherwise have to be built: automatic reconnection in the browser, Last-Event-ID replay, and passage through any HTTP proxy with no upgrade handshake. The bus keeps a bounded ring buffer per workspace. A client that reconnects inside the buffer is replayed; one that has been away longer gets an explicit resync directive telling it to refetch over REST. Silently skipping the gap would leave a dashboard confidently displaying stale numbers, which is a worse failure than a reload. The frame format and every field are on the event contract page.

Repost an event, a batch or a whole report — nothing duplicates and no count moves. This is not a nicety: CI steps get retried, networks time out after the server has already committed, and a publisher that cannot retry safely is a publisher that loses data. (source, event id) is unique in the store, so an individual event can only ever be applied once. X-Idempotency-Key covers a whole batch. POST /api/v1/runs with a run_id you chose returns the existing run instead of creating a second one. The canonical JSON adapter derives event ids as a UUIDv5 over (source, run_id, sequence, type), so importing the same file twice against the same run applies zero new events. shell The same batch, posted twice $ curl -sX POST "$HUB/api/v1/runs/$RUN/events" -H 'X-Idempotency-Key: batch-1' -d @events.jso

d.h: Run comparison against the previous comparable run
d.x: "47 failures" means nothing on its own. "3 newly failing, 44 still failing, 2 newly passing" means somebody broke three things and the other 44 were already broken. Every run is compared against the previous comparable run — the same project, team, component, test type, environment and branch. That is the narrowest slice that makes the comparison honest: comparing a staging e2e run against a unit run on a feature branch would produce a delta that means nothing. The comparison names newly failing, newly passing, still failing, added and removed tests by identity, plus deltas on pass rate, duration and total.

d.h: Flaky detection, two definitions, both written down
d.x: Within a run, a test is flaky when it both failed and succeeded across its attempts in that one run. Across runs, it is flaky when it disagreed with its own recent history. Both formulas are implemented exactly once, in test_hub.domain.metrics, and nothing else in the codebase is allowed to compute one — so no two parts of the product can disagree about the same number. The formulas.

d.h: Two altitudes, kept apart on purpose
d.x: The overview answers "how is the portfolio doing" and is cheap enough to poll. The run and test pages are the engineering drill-down and are allowed to return a lot. They are separate endpoints and separate payload types, so that making the drill-down richer cannot make the front page slower. The analytics page sits between them and pays a bounded price for it: it reads the five most recent finished runs in full — enough for "what keeps breaking" to be a pattern rather than one run's luck — caches them, because a finished run cannot change, and never mixes in a run that is still going.

Two adapters ship in the box: JUnit/xUnit XML, and Test Hub's own canonical JSON. Both are registered through the test_hub.adapters entry-point group — exactly the mechanism a third-party package uses. There is no privileged internal path, which means the plugin API is the one we ourselves have to live with. Test Hub deliberately does not advertise support for "any JSON" or "any XML". An adapter that guesses produces silently wrong numbers, and a wrong pass rate is worse than a failed import. Unknown input returns a 415 that lists every installed adapter. Writing one.

Test Hub ingests untrusted text — test output routinely contains credentials, HTML and things that look like markup — and renders it in a browser. The defaults assume that: Loopback binding Binding anywhere else requires authentication or an explicit --insecure-no-auth that warns on every start. There is no silent path to an open Test Hub on a network. Hashed tokens PBKDF2-SHA256. The plaintext exists once, in the output of test-hub token create. A stolen database is a list of digests. Entity-free XML Parsed through defusedxml: DTDs and external entities are refused, not expanded. Billion-laughs and XXE fixtures are in the test suite. d.h: No Node, no CDN, no build step
d.x: The frontend is hand-written CSS and classic (non-module) JavaScript shipped inside the wheel. Charts are inline SVG drawn by hand. This is not asceticism, it buys three specific things: the CSP can forbid remote origins outright; a Python package that needs npm to build is a packaging liability; and a dashboard that fetches nothing from the internet renders identically on an air-gapped network and cannot quietly start leaking a request to a font host. The same rule applies to this documentation site. It loads nothing from the internet either.

d.h: Deliberately not in the first release
d.x: Named, with the extension points left in place, because a feature list that only lists features is a sales document: Test authoring or manual test management. Test execution and orchestration — Test Hub reads results, it does not run tests. AI failure analysis. SSO, SAML and SCIM. Full multi-tenancy. Every row already carries a workspace_id; there is one workspace and no UI to change it. Kubernetes manifests, licence enforcement, notifications and issue-tracker integrations. Two known limits of the first release are documented rather than hidden: single-process write throughput, and an in-process SSE bus that stops one Uvicorn worker from becoming four. Where each one starts to bite.

Five views, three altitudes. The overview answers how the portfolio is doing, analytics answers what keeps going wrong, and the run and test pages answer why something went red. This walks each one, and says what a panel means rather than what it is called.

Every view shares a navigation rail — the brand, Overview, Analytics and Runs, with the dark-mode switch at its foot — and a top bar carrying a relative timestamp of the last refresh, a connection indicator and the settings menu. Below 860px the rail becomes a bar: a phone has no width to spare for a permanent column. The connection indicator has three states — Connecting, Live and Reconnecting. In live mode it reflects the Server-Sent Events stream: green and "Live" means results are arriving as they happen. When the stream drops, a banner appears above the view and the dashboard keeps working from what it already has; it reconnects by itself, and if it has been away long enough for the server's replay buffer to have moved past it, it refetches instead of quietly displaying stale numbers.
The executive altitude. It answers four questions and refuses to answer any others: how much testing happened, how much of it passed, is it getting better or worse, and what is on fire right now.

A segmented control picks the window — 7, 14, 30 or 90 days — and six filters narrow it: project, team, component, test type, environment and branch. The dropdown values are facets the server computes from the data that is actually there, so you are never offered a filter that matches nothing. The same filter vocabulary is used on the Runs view, which is what lets a selection carry from one to the other.

Six tiles: Tests, Passed, Failed, Error, Skipped and Running. Two things about them are deliberate and worth knowing. They count tests, not runs — the run count is the sub-label under "Tests". And a pass rate with nothing executed renders as an em dash rather than 0%. A suite that only skipped is not a 0% suite, and showing it in red trains people to ignore red.

A full-width chart directly under the KPI tiles, and the one on the page that never stops moving. Time runs along the bottom, with now at the right-hand edge. The moment a run starts — any project, from CI or from a laptop — a bar pops up at that edge, stacked by status, and grows while the run's results arrive: what has finished at the bottom, the tests still running in blue on top, with a pulsing dot above while the run is live. Then the whole chart glides left with the clock, once a second, so a run you saw start a minute ago is a minute's width further along. Each bar is a slot of time — fifteen seconds, a minute, five minutes or half an hour, depending on the span — and every run that started in that slot stacks into it, so six jobs fanned out by one pipeline are one taller bar rather

One full-width row, one bar per project: each project's newest run in the window, stacked to 100% by status, with its pass rate and test count at the end of the bar. A run from CI and a run from a laptop count the same — the line under the project's name says which it was ( Push, Pull request, Schedule, Local, Manual …) and how long ago. Hover a bar, or tab to its project, for every status with its count and share; the name links to the run. It moves while a run is in flight. A run that is still going is its project's status: it is marked Live, the tests not yet finished are drawn last, in blue, so the bar fills up from the left, and each result that arrives redraws it within a couple of seconds, without a refresh. d.h: Outcomes, health, volume, trend and duration
d.x: Test outcomes — the run's status mix as a single proportional bar, in the status colours, with a legend. Statuses with a zero count are omitted rather than drawn as slivers. Health — the headline pass rate for the window, with the counts spelled out underneath in a sentence. Volume by day — tests executed per day. This is the chart that tells you a suite stopped running before it tells you the suite started failing. Pass rate trend — pass rate and failure rate per day across the window. Run duration — p50 and p95 per day. Both, because a mean hides the shard that takes eleven minutes. These charts are inline SVG, drawn by the dashboard itself, reading their palette back out of the CSS custom properties. That is why they re-colour correctly the instant you switch theme, and why there is no

Active runs lists what is queued or running right now, and is the panel the demo data deliberately keeps one run open for. When nothing is running it says so rather than showing an empty table. Project health is one row per project: runs in the last 24 hours, last run and its status, pass rate with a delta against the previous period, live runs, and a count of flaky tests. Below that, the worst offenders — the tests failing most often, and the flakiest — each linking straight to its test page. An empty overview that is not an empty install If every run in the workspace is older than the selected window, the overview says exactly that instead of rendering a blank state that looks like a fresh installation. The overview says how the portfolio is doing. Analytics sits one level below it and answers the four questions that come immediately afterwards: what broke, where, whose it is, and what it costs. It reads the five most recent finished runs that match the filters, in full, plus the same overview payload the dashboard uses. In full is the point — failure taxonomy, ownership and per-test timings need every attempt of every test, and no summary carries those. Runs still in flight are skipped: half a run's failures classified as if they were all of them is a wrong answer, not a partial one. Finished runs cannot change, so their payloads are cached and a live update costs one overview request.

Six numbers, each with the sentence that stops it being misread. Stability score is the pass rate less the share of executed tests that flaked — a suite where everything passes on the second attempt is not a healthy suite, and a pass rate alone says it is. Pass rate, last run carries its delta against the previous comparable run. Flaky tests, failing in the last run, runs analysed and time in tests complete the row.

Failures grouped by the exception that raised them, ordered by weight, each with the tests behind it. Forty failures that are all one AssertionError in one fixture is one bug; forty spread over six exception types is six — and that distinction is the whole reason the card exists. A test that failed the same way in four of the five runs carries a multiplier rather than appearing four times, and a type containing something that was passing in the previous run is marked new. Failures the framework did not classify are filed as Unclassified, never under the test's own name, which would give every failure its own bucket and turn the taxonomy into a list.

Suite hotspots stacks failing results against everything else for the busiest suites. Who owns what is the same numbers per owner, with everything unclaimed counted honestly as unclaimed rather than hidden. Where the time goes sums each test's duration across those runs by its stable identity: a test that takes four seconds every run costs twenty seconds of the last five, and that — not its single worst appearance — is what decides whether it is worth fixing.

The one card on the page that is about the window rather than the recent runs. Each test gets one cell per recent run, oldest on the left, and one of four words: stable (passed every time it ran), flaky (both passed and failed), broken (has not passed) and quiet (too few runs to say). The order is deliberate: a test that has never passed is not a flaky test, it is an unfinished one.

Every run, newest first, with the full filter set: a free-text search over run name, branch, commit and tags, plus project, team, component, test type, environment, branch and status. Sort and page are here too. All of it lives in the URL. That is the feature, not tidiness: a filtered list has to be a link somebody can paste, and it has to survive a reload and the back button. The view does not know how sorting is done — it puts sort and dir in the hash, and the provider honours them on the server where it can and in the browser where a filter the API cannot express forced it to fetch a page and refine it. The table says which. Each row carries the run's status, project, team and component, its environment and branch, the framework and language if the publisher said, the counts, the durati

d.x: The engineering altitude: what a person needs when a pipeline has just gone red.

Where the run came from — framework and version, language, environment, branch, commit, CI provider, pipeline id and a link to the pipeline, hostname, OS, and who started it. Every field is optional, because publishers know varying amounts, and the panel shows what it was told rather than inventing placeholders.

The panel that earns its place. It shows deltas for pass rate, duration and test count, then five lists: List What it means Newly failing Passed in the baseline, fails now. This is the list you read first. Still failing Was already broken. Not your regression, but not nothing. Newly passing Was broken, is fixed. Added Test identities that did not exist in the baseline run. Removed Identities the baseline had and this run did not report — deleted, renamed, or not collected. The baseline is the previous comparable run: same project, team, component, test type, environment and branch. When there is no such run the panel says so, in those words, rather than comparing against something unlike it and producing a delta that means nothing. There is a link to open the baseline. If the import could not represent something exactly, it is on this panel: severity, code, message and where in the input it happened. An unmapped status word, a timestamp with no UTC offset, a truncated stack trace, counts that disagreed with the file's own header. Nothing is swallowed, because a warning you cannot see is a number you cannot trust.

The suite tree, with each suite's counts and duration, expandable to the tests inside it. Below that, every test in the run as a searchable, sortable table: status (with a flaky pill where it applies), name, parameters, attempt count and duration. The table's own search, status filter and sort are view-local rather than in the URL: they are a way of reading one page, not a place anybody links to. The run itself, and every test on it, are linkable.

Files attached to the run — screenshots, videos, logs, traces, coverage, and the raw uploaded report if store_raw_reports is on. They are stored content-addressed, so the same screenshot uploaded from fifty parallel shards is one stored object. They are always served as an attachment with the stored content type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, never inline: an artifact is attacker-supplied content sitting on the dashboard's own origin.

d.h: Test detail — one test, across every run
d.x: This page exists because identity is stable. A test that got a new id every run would have no history, could not be called flaky, and could not be compared with itself.

Flake rate, failure rate, average duration with a small duration trend, and the attempt count in the latest run. Flake rate is the percentage of runs in the trailing window in which this test behaved flakily — it was flaky within that run, or its outcome disagreed with the window's majority. Fewer than two usable runs and it renders as nothing at all: one data point cannot describe consistency.

Every attempt gets its own panel, in order, each with its status, the framework's original word for that status where it differed, the duration, the failure type and message, the stack trace, and any stdout, stderr or captured logs. A retry is a separate execution with its own output, not a correction of the one before it — so the failure that a rerun later "fixed" is still on the page. That is the argument for the event model, made visible. The bytes are the bytes Stack traces, logs and stdout arrive as text nodes inside a 
. There is no formatting pass, no ANSI translation and no markup: what the framework produced is what you read. A test named  renders as that text, and there is a test asserting it.

A strip of squares, newest on the left, one per run, each coloured by outcome and linking to its run — the shape of a flaky test is visible at a glance. Underneath, the same history as a table: run time, status, attempt count, duration, branch and environment.

Seven commands, one of which has two sub-commands. None of them holds any logic of its own — each is a thin wrapper over the same service layer the HTTP API calls, which is why anything you can do here you can also do over HTTP. Everything below was run against test-hub 0.1.0; the outputs are copied out of a terminal, not paraphrased.

d.h: The shape of the command line
d.x: Every command takes -h or --help, and the root command takes -V / --version. The version line reports two numbers, because they move independently: the package version, and the canonical schema version that every payload carries. shell $ test-hub --version test-hub 0.1.0 (canonical schema v1) output test-hub --help, commands only serve Start the API and serve the dashboard. ingest Import a report file into the local store. publish Send a report to a remote Test Hub server. demo Populate the store with realistic sample data. prune Delete runs older than a retention cutoff. formats List the installed report adapters. token Create and hash API tokens. Sub-commands are registered lazily, inside a function, so test-hub --help does not import FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and every adapter to print seven

d.h: There is no --token flag, on purpose
d.x: Neither publish nor token hash will take a token as an argument. This is not an oversight to be worked around; it is the one rule that shows up in every command that touches a credential. ps is world-readable. On a shared build agent, every other user on the box can read the full argument vector of every running process. A token on a command line is a token handed to anyone with a shell on that machine. Shell history keeps it. ~/.bash_history and ~/.zsh_history are written on exit, are rarely encrypted, and are frequently backed up. CI logs echo commands. Most runners print the command before running it, and those logs are often readable by more people than the secret store is. d.h: What happens when a value is wrong
d.x: Settings are validated at construction, so a bad value stops the process rather than producing a subtly wrong runtime. The bounds are real — max_report_bytes has a floor of 1024, flaky_window_runs a floor of 2, port a range of 1–65535, and log_level / log_format are closed sets. output TEST_HUB_LOG_LEVEL=verbose, last lines of the traceback ValidationError: 1 validation error for Settings log_level Input should be 'debug', 'info', 'warning' or 'error' [type=literal_error, input_value='verbose', input_type=str] Honest about the presentation The message names the setting and the acceptable values, which is what you need. But it arrives as a Pydantic traceback and exits 1, not as the clean error: line and exit 78 that ConfigurationError produces — settings are validated before the CLI's error

A laptop Nothing. The defaults are loopback, unauthenticated and stored under your user-data directory, which is correct for a machine only you can reach. A shared server TEST_HUB_API_TOKEN_HASHES (which turns auth on by itself), --host 0.0.0.0 behind a proxy that terminates TLS, TEST_HUB_TRUSTED_HOSTS set to the name that proxy serves, TEST_HUB_LOG_FORMAT=json, and TEST_HUB_ROOT_PATH if it lives on a sub-path. A bearer token over plain HTTP across a network is a token you have given away.

The API is the product. It is designed so that curl is a first-class publisher — no client library is required, and every example on this page is a plain HTTP request you can paste into a terminal. All endpoints are versioned under /api/v1. /healthz deliberately is not: it is infrastructure, and a container healthcheck should not need updating when the API version moves. The machine-readable contract is served by the running instance: /api/openapi.json, with browsable documentation at /api/docs and /api/redoc.

Off by default, because the default bind is loopback. It turns itself on as soon as any token is configured. Then every write needs one: shell curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_HUB_TOKEN" … curl -H "X-API-Key: $TEST_HUB_TOKEN" … # same token, same check X-API-Key is accepted because a surprising number of CI systems make it awkward to set an Authorization header on a generic HTTP step. Reads stay open even with authentication on — the common deployment is "anyone in the team may look, only CI may write". Set TEST_HUB_REQUIRE_AUTH_FOR_READS=true to close them too.

Every failing endpoint returns the same shape, so a client needs exactly one error parser: json { "error": "unknown_format", "message": "no installed adapter recognised this file", "detail": { "installed_adapters": [ …] } } Status error Means 401 unauthorized Missing, malformed or wrong token. The message is identical for all three on purpose. 403 forbidden Authenticated but not allowed. 404 not_found No such run, test or artifact. 409 conflict A write contradicted one that already landed. 413 payload_too_large Over a configured size limit. 415 unknown_format No adapter recognised the input. detail lists every installed one. 422 validation_error, adapter_error The body did not match the schema, or the format was recognised but unparseable.

Every write is idempotent, twice over: at the event level through a UNIQUE(source, event_id) constraint, and at the batch level through an optional X-Idempotency-Key header. Reposting returns applied: 0 and moves no count. Retry freely — CI steps get retried, and a network timeout after the server already committed is a normal Tuesday.

Cheap enough for a container healthcheck every ten seconds, and it touches the database — a Test Hub that cannot read its own store is not healthy, however well it serves HTTP. Unauthenticated, and contains no secrets, so it is safe to paste into an issue. shell Real response $ curl -s localhost:8000/healthz { "status": "ok", "version": "0.1.0", "schema_version": 1, "database": "ok", "workspace_id": "b037a4b3-53f8-5326-a5d5-f5fad3c31052", "live_subscribers": 0, "time": "2026-09-09T03:44:29.301538Z" } workspace_id is here because a publisher cannot invent it and events carry it — the Python SDK fetches it from this endpoint once and caches it.

Append results as they happen. Set "sequence": 0 on every event to have the server allocate a contiguous block; send your own monotonic numbers if you want gap detection, which you probably do for a long-running suite.

shell curl -X POST "localhost:8000/api/v1/runs/$RUN/finish" \ -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}' An empty body is the normal case. An adapter turns bytes into a stream of domain events. That is the whole job — it never touches the database, never learns that HTTP exists, and never decides what a run is called. This page is the protocol, the six rules that are not negotiable, and a working third-party package that was installed into a real environment to write it.

d.h: The protocol, and where the seam is
d.x: Everything Test Hub can read arrives through one interface, and it produces domain events — nothing else. It is a Protocol, so there is no base class you are obliged to inherit and no registration ceremony beyond a single entry point: python test_hub.adapters.base class ReportAdapter(Protocol): name: str def detect(self, stream: IO[bytes], filename: str | None, content_type: str | None) -> float:... def parse(self, stream: IO[bytes], context: ParseContext) -> Iterable[DomainEvent]:... The seam is deliberately narrow, and the narrowness is what buys two things. An adapter is unit-testable against a fixture file with no server, no database and no event loop — the test suite further down runs in 0.07 seconds. And the file-import path and the live-publishing path share every line of code after

Because ReportAdapter is structural, inheriting is a convenience and never a requirement — a plain class with the two methods is a perfectly good adapter. d.h: Detection, and what each score actually means
d.x: detect returns a confidence in [0.0, 1.0]. The registry asks every installed adapter in name order, rewinding the stream between each one, and keeps the highest score at or above MIN_CONFIDENCE, which is 0.3. Ties break on priority and then on name, so two adapters that both answer 0.9 resolve identically on every machine and in every process rather than according to whichever entry point importlib.metadata happened to yield first. Score What it means Example 0.0 Definitely not mine. Return this rather than raising. The stream starts with < and your format is JSON. 0.3 The filename extension or the content type fits, and nothing else was checked. This is the floor for selection: a file can be chosen on its name alone, but only when nothing claims it harder. results.hopper whose content cou

Never raise. Return 0.0. A detector that throws is caught, logged at warning level and scored 0.0 anyway, but the log line is noise nobody needs. Read a few kilobytes, not the file. BaseAdapter.sniff(stream) reads SNIFF_BYTES (8192) and rewinds. The registry rewinds between adapters too, so you are not obliged to be tidy — but an adapter that reads 200 MB to make up its mind makes every import on the server slow, including the ones it loses. Never claim “any JSON” or “any XML”. This is the rule with teeth, and it has its own section below.

d.h: Why an adapter must not claim arbitrary JSON or XML
d.x: An adapter that answers 0.6 for every JSON object will swallow coverage reports, ESLint output and half of somebody's package.json. Each of those then arrives as a run with a plausible-looking pass rate that is silently wrong, and a wrong pass rate on a dashboard is worse than an import that failed, because nobody goes looking for it. Require a discriminator your format actually has. d.h: Stream; do not build a DOM
d.x: Use iterparse with elem.clear(), and detach each finished element from its parent as soon as you have turned it into events. The built-in JUnit adapter holds one suite's worth of elements plus the event it is currently yielding, whatever the file's size. A 200 MB Surefire aggregate parsed into a DOM is a multi-gigabyte resident set and an out-of-memory kill, which to whoever is watching looks like Test Hub crashing rather than like a large upload.

d.h: Two more, less dramatic and no less real
d.x: Do not build a path from anything in the file. The artifact store refuses names containing separators,.., NUL bytes or Windows device names outright rather than repairing them. If you emit artifact.published events, reduce a reported filename to its last component first. Do not trust the file's own totals. tests="200" failures="3" is advisory and frequently wrong — a partially uploaded shard, a framework that counts retries, a hand-edited file. Counts are folded from the cases actually parsed. Emit a counts_mismatch warning when the file disagrees with you, rather than hiding the disagreement or, worse, believing it.

d.x: Everything that crosses a boundary — an HTTP response, the output of an adapter — is one of a small set of Pydantic models. Database rows are never serialized directly. This page is that contract: what is promised, what is derived, and what a publisher in any language has to reproduce to interoperate. The models live in test_hub.domain.models and are the public wire contract. The SQLAlchemy rows on disk are a separate, private thing, and nothing ever serializes an ORM object. That separation is what lets the table layout change — a new index, a split table, PostgreSQL — without a version bump that every consumer has to react to.

One integer, defined once in test_hub/version.py. It moves independently of the package version and only on a breaking change. shell Both numbers, from two places that cost nothing to ask $ test-hub --version test-hub 0.1.0 (canonical schema v1) $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0","schema_version":1,"database":"ok", "workspace_id":"b037a4b3-53f8-5326-a5d5-f5fad3c31052","live_subscribers":0, "time":"2026-09-09T03:30:44.034812Z"} /healthz is the cheapest way for a consumer to find out what a server speaks before sending it anything.

Only the ones allowed to cross a version boundary on their own — a top-level document a consumer might have received with no surrounding context. Carries schema_version Does not TestRun, RunDetail, TestDetail, OverviewSnapshot, ImportResult, and DomainEvent (as schemaversion, following the CloudEvents attribute-naming rules) Workspace, Project, RunSummary, RunCounts, TestSuite, TestCase, TestAttempt, Artifact, RunComparison, TestHistoryPoint, TrendPoint, ProjectHealth, ParserWarning, FailureDetail, RunContext A TestCase is only ever seen inside a RunDetail, so stamping a version onto it would put the same integer on every one of ten thousand objects in the same document.

Within a major schema version: Fields may be added. A new optional field on any model is not a breaking change, so a consumer must tolerate one. Fields are not removed, renamed or retyped. The meaning of a field does not change. In particular the metric definitions are part of this contract rather than an implementation detail: changing what pass_rate counts is a version bump even though the field's name and type are untouched. Enum members may be added. TestStatus, RunStatus, TestType, TriggerType and ArtifactKind are closed sets for this version, but the honest reading is that a future release could add one. Treat an unrecognized member the way you would treat unknown or other, not as a crash. Anything else — a removed field, a changed formula, a new event type, a different envelope shap

A test's identity has to survive being re-run, re-ordered, re-parameterized in a different order, moved to a different line and executed on another machine by a different framework version. If it does not, every run invents a new set of tests, and history, comparison and flakiness are all worthless. Three identities are therefore derived rather than assigned, as UUIDv5 in one fixed namespace: python TEST_HUB_NAMESPACE = uuid.UUID("4c8f4c4d-3ecb-5f78-a1e4-c1a24e07b1e6") Identity Hashed input workspace "workspace" \x1f slug.lower() suite "suite" \x1f project \x1f suite_path test project \x1f suite_path \x1f class_name \x1f test_name \x1f params The namespace is hard-coded and must never move: every historical identity would change with it. \x1f is the ASCII unit separator, chosen because it

d.h: What is in it, and what is deliberately kept out
d.x: In the identity Deliberately excluded Because project key timestamps Every run has different ones. suite path line numbers and file offsets Adding an import above a test would rename it. class name durations They are the measurement, not the subject. test name worker or shard id, hostname Re-sharding a suite would mint a whole new set of tests. normalized parameters run id, build number, branch A test's history is precisely the thing that has to span these.

Each component is normalized to Unicode NFC, has its whitespace collapsed, and is stripped; suite paths are converted to forward slashes with a leading./ removed. Parameter values are rendered with their volatile fragments scrubbed: <Foo object at 0x7f3c…> becomes object at 0x?, a bare UUID becomes <uuid>, and a long hex literal becomes 0x?. They are replaced with a stable token rather than dropped, so that two genuinely different parameters do not collide. Every write into Test Hub becomes a domain event, and events are the only thing that changes state. This page is the wire contract: what the envelope looks like on the network, what each of the eight types carries, and exactly what happens when you post the same thing twice. A JUnit XML file dropped on the CLI, a POST /api/v1/imports from a Jenkins job and a live publisher streaming results as they happen all converge on the same list of events and the same apply_events call. Nothing else in the codebase writes a run, a test or an attempt. That is what makes reposting safe, what makes a retry a fact rather than an overwrite, and what makes the counts recomputable from the log at any time. d.h: Why xfailed is a success and xpassed is not
d.x: A test marked expected-to-fail that failed did exactly what it was declared to do. Colouring it red trains people to ignore red, which is the most expensive failure mode a test dashboard has. d.x: Every row carries workspace_id from the first migration — so the column never has to be added to a populated events table later — but the open-source edition creates exactly one workspace, derives its id from the slug, and offers no way to create or select another. require_read and require_write do not consider the workspace at all. Nothing records which token wrote which run, when, or from where. The events table records source — a publisher-supplied string that anyone can set to anything — and received_at. No per-token quota, no per-IP throttle, no concurrency cap on imports. A publisher stuck in a retry loop is limited only by the size caps above and by SQLite's single-writer ceiling — which under load means everyone else's imports queue behind it. If the port is reachable by anything you do not control, put a rate limit in the proxy.

d.h: Does it work with my framework?
d.x: If it can write JUnit/xUnit XML — pytest, JUnit, Surefire, Gradle, Jest, Playwright, PHPUnit, gotestsum, Mocha, and most others — yes, today, with no plugin. If it cannot, write Test Hub's canonical JSON from a twenty-line script, or write an adapter. Test Hub deliberately does not claim to accept "any JSON" or "any XML". A format that guesses produces silently wrong numbers, which is worse than a refusal. Unrecognised input returns a 415 listing what this server does accept.

d.h: Do I need Python on the build agent?
d.x: No. The REST API is the product and curl is a first-class publisher: shell curl -X POST "$HUB/api/v1/imports" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_HUB_TOKEN" \ -F "file=@results.xml" -F "project=payments-api" -F "type=component" The Python SDK is a convenience for people who already have Python, never a requirement.

d.h: What happens if I publish the same report twice?
d.x: Without a --run-id, you get two runs — which is correct, because two genuine executions of the same suite are two runs. With the same --run-id, the second import applies zero events and changes no count: shell $ test-hub ingest report.json -p storefront-web --run-id 3f2a91c4-… --json | jq '{events_applied, events_ignored}' { "events_applied": 0, "events_ignored": 12 } Every write is idempotent twice over: UNIQUE(source, event_id) at the event level, and X-Idempotency-Key at the batch level. Retry freely.

d.h: How do I make four parallel shards into one run?
d.x: Generate a UUID once before the shards start and pass it to every one as --run-id. Order does not matter, and re-running a single shard is safe. Worked examples for both GitHub Actions and Jenkins.

d.h: Why does my pass rate show as "—"?
d.x: Because nothing executed. The pass-rate denominator excludes skipped and cancelled tests, so a run where everything was skipped has no pass rate at all. Showing 0% would read as total failure, which is the opposite of the truth. See Metrics.

d.h: Why does a retried test count once?
d.x: Because it is one test. A retry is recorded as a second attempt, never as a second test and never as an overwrite of the first. The test contributes once to the counts through its last attempt, so a test that failed and then passed is green — and because the earlier attempt is still there, it is also flaky. Counting it twice would inflate the total and make the pass rate wrong.

d.h: A test shows 100% flake rate but its history is all green. Why?
d.x: Because it passes only when it is retried. Flakiness is measured two ways: within a run (the attempts disagreed) and across runs (the outcome disagreed with its own history). A test that fails then passes on every single run is green every time and flaky every time — which is exactly the thing worth telling you about.

d.h: Why does it refuse to start on 0.0.0.0?
d.x: Because you did not configure authentication, and a Test Hub reachable from a network with no authentication lets anyone who can reach the port read and write every test result. Either create a token, or say --insecure-no-auth and accept a warning on every start. There is no silent path to an open instance.

d.h: Where does the data live, and how big does it get?
d.x: Under TEST_HUB_DATA_DIR — a platform data directory by default, listed in Configuration. One SQLite file — or a PostgreSQL database, if you chose one — plus a content-addressed artifacts/ tree. Size is driven almost entirely by captured output, not by test counts: a run of a few thousand tests with no logs is small, and one test with a 200 KiB stack trace is not. Text fields are capped by TEST_HUB_MAX_TEXT_FIELD_BYTES (256 KiB by default) and truncation is flagged rather than silent. Artifacts are deduplicated by SHA-256, so fifty shards uploading the same screenshot store one copy.

Set TEST_HUB_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname — after pip install "test-hub[postgres]", or with the Docker image, which already has the driver — and Test Hub uses PostgreSQL instead of SQLite. Nothing else changes, and Choosing a database has the Compose override and the details. SQLite remains the default, and for one Test Hub it is also the faster of the two: imports are bound by the process's CPU, and SQLite answers in-process. Choose PostgreSQL for what a database server gives you — managed backups, replication, a database other tools can query — and as the groundwork for running more than one Test Hub process, which is where its concurrent writers would pay.

d.h: Why is there no Node, no bundler, no framework?
d.x: Three reasons, in order of how much they mattered: a Content-Security-Policy of default-src 'none' is only possible with no inline scripts and no remote origins; a Python package that needs npm to build is a packaging liability; and the whole application is about fifteen small files, which does not need a framework. The dashboard fetches nothing from the internet either, so an air-gapped install renders exactly like a connected one. CI fails the build if any src or href in the page points off-origin.

The live-update bus is in-process. Two workers would hold two buses, and half the connected dashboards would miss half the events. There is deliberately no --workers flag. Replacing the bus with Redis Streams or NATS is the fix, and the EventBus protocol is where it goes.

d.h: What is deliberately not in this release?
d.x: Test authoring or manual test management; test execution and orchestration; AI-generated failure analysis; SSO, SAML and SCIM; full multi-tenancy; Kubernetes manifests; licence enforcement; and notifications or issue-tracker integrations. The extension points are in place for several of these — every row is scoped to a workspace from the first migration, and authentication sits behind an interface — but none of them were allowed to delay a working vertical slice.

d.h: How does it compare with what I already have?
d.x: If one framework in one repository is all you have, a per-framework HTML reporter is simpler and you should use one. Test Hub earns its place when results arrive from several languages, several teams and several pipelines, and nobody can answer "is the suite healthier than last week?" without opening six tabs.
